evidence.text:
蘇子高事平
王庾諸公欲用孔廷尉爲丹陽
亂離之後百姓彫弊孔慨然曰昔肅祖臨崩諸君親
升御牀並蒙眷識共奉遺詔孔坦疎賤不在顧命之
列既有艱難則以微臣爲先今猶爼上腐肉任人膾
截耳於是拂衣而去諸公亦

judgment.explanation: 王隱 is the historian Wang Yin, author of the Jin Shu (晉書). The annotation cites 按王隱晉書蘇峻事, referring to Wang Yin's Jin Shu on the Su Jun affair. The candidate 王隱 matches the canonical name and role as historian/author.
蘇峻 is the full name of Su Jun, the rebel leader. The annotation cites Wang Yin's Jin Shu on the Su Jun affair (蘇峻事). The candidate 蘇峻 matches the canonical name.
峻 is the single-character personal name of 蘇峻 (Su Jun). The annotation describes 峻 and 碩 still holding Stone City. The candidate 蘇峻 matches.

坦 refers to 孔坦 (Kong Tan), but the supplied candidate is a local candidate person '坦' with no canonical identity linking to the historical Kong Tan. The candidate is a source-grounded local form, not an existing person record for Kong Tan. The likely referent 孔坦 is not among the supplied candidates as an existing person.

review.explanation: The mention 王隱 appears in annotation-004 as '按王隱晉書蘇峻事', explicitly citing Wang Yin's Jin Shu. The surface form matches the canonical name exactly, and the role as historian/author of Jin Shu is consistent with the annotation context. The distinctness from Su Jun and Kong Tan is correctly noted. No contradicting evidence exists.

The mention 蘇峻 appears in annotation-004 as part of '按王隱晉書蘇峻事', referring to the Su Jun affair. The surface form matches the canonical name exactly. The coreference chain linking 蘇峻 to 蘇子高 (main text) and 峻 (annotations) is consistent with the historical figure Su Jun, the rebel leader. The annotation-001 explicitly identifies 峻 as 蘇峻's brother 碩's sibling context, and annotation-002 continues the narrative about 峻 and 碩 holding Stone City. No contradicting evidence.

The mention 峻 in annotation-002 ('峻碩猶據石頭潰') refers to Su Jun via abbreviated name. Annotation-001 establishes 峻 as 蘇峻 (the rebel leader) and 碩 as his brother. The coreference chain linking this mention to the full-name mention 蘇峻 (sfh1-mention-35576ea21c749384ae533344) is well-supported by the annotation context. The distinctness from 碩 (sfh1-mention-aa2241c61bbc24ff463603d2) is correctly noted since 碩 is Su Jun's brother. No contradicting evidence.

The mention 蘇子高 appears in the main text ('蘇子高事平'). The alias registry maps 蘇子高 (surname + courtesy name) to 蘇峻. The main text describes the aftermath of Su Jun's rebellion ('事平' = affair settled), which is consistent with the historical Su Jun. The annotation-004 explicitly references '蘇峻事' in the same story, confirming the identity. While the reference_semantics reports low confidence due to a failed semantic record, the alias registry match plus the strong contextual evidence from the annotations supports the resolution. No contradicting evidence.

The candidate evidence from people.json provides the canonical name 蘇峻. The annotation directly supports the identification of 峻 as Su Jun.

assertions.interpretation: The scene is set after the rebellion of Su Jun (蘇峻, styled 子高) was pacified, marking the temporal context for the subsequent events.
After the chaos and upheaval of the rebellion, the people were impoverished—this describes the state of affairs at the time of the scene.
At this point in the scene, Kong Tan flung his sleeves and left—marking the immediate sequence of events.
The annotation records that at the beginning of Emperor Mingdi's reign there was a ballad saying 'the high mountain collapses'—a prophecy/omen context from an earlier period.
The annotation notes that afterwards the various lords were executed—a later outcome following the events described.
The annotation records that they scattered and fled, were pursued and beheaded—a later outcome of the rebellion's suppression.
The annotation notes that Su Jun and Su Shuo still held Stone City before it collapsed—a later phase of the rebellion's end.
The annotation (citing Wang Yin's Jin shu on the Su Jun affair) records that after pacification, Tao Kan wanted to employ Kong Tan—a subsequent development.
